Understanding Jev-Style System One Models:
Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?

Mingyang Song    Mao Zheng    Zhiyuan Ma    Xinpeng Zhou Affiliation: Foundation Model Department, Tencent, China Email: nickmysong@tencent.com Affiliation:  nick7nlp/Jev-Selection-Bias
Abstract

Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev’s accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27.3–28.5% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. Reordering loses substantially more initial successes than fixed-order repetition, a gap that also appears in highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.

1 Introduction

A correct choice should depend on candidate content, yet language models can change their answers when only the presentation changes. Reordering options can alter multiple-choice answers (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Zheng et al., 2024), and swapping two unchanged responses can reverse an LLM judge’s preference (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Song et al., 2025). Such selection bias lets presentation influence a decision without adding evidence about which candidate is correct. A question answered correctly in one order may therefore fail in another.

Prompting alone does not reliably remove this bias. Zheng et al. (2024) find residual bias under explicit debiasing instructions and chain-of-thought prompting in the settings tested. Calibration and targeted training offer ways to reduce it (Li et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2026), while evidence from multi-document question answering suggests that reasoning models can be less position-biased (Li et al., 2026). Selection bias is therefore sensitive to how a model is trained and used. This raises the possibility that models designed expressly for candidate selection could better preserve correct choices across presentations.

Jev-style System One models make this possibility concrete. They predict a probability distribution directly over candidates supplied with each request. TypeSafe describes Jev as trained for calibrated decisions through Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).11 1 TypeSafe’s model introduction and machine-learning primer describe this training goal; the complete architecture and training recipe remain proprietary. Recent efforts to reproduce this behavior have produced a growing family of models (Geuter et al., 2026; Li and Wagle, 2026; Zhuang et al., 2026), which we call Jev reproductions. These implementations range from training a decision head with backbone adaptation to extracting candidate probabilities from a frozen LLM. The term denotes a shared behavioral goal, without implying recovery of Jev’s proprietary internals or a common architecture. Candidate representation, probability readout, and decision-specific learning are therefore possible sources of robustness, not guarantees of it.

Existing evidence already challenges the assumption that structured decisions resist bias. Typed decision models can repeat pairwise judgments reliably yet reverse them when the two responses are swapped (Lukassen et al., 2026). In public Jev-style implementations, option labels can override written definitions, and serialization changes can alter this behavior with model weights fixed (Azizi et al., 2026). What remains limited is a systematic comparison of Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs as correct choices face repeated reordering in multi-option tasks. A single swap cannot reveal how widely failures spread over further orders, and aggregate accuracy can hide losses that recoveries offset. We therefore ask: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias?

We investigate this question with a simple test that shuffles options while preserving question and candidate content. The study compares two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs on SuperGPQA (M-A-P et al., 2025), LEXam (Fan et al., 2026), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), and GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2023). Our primary collection pools 1,700 questions from SuperGPQA and LEXam. For each question, we compare the original order, its reversal, and six random permutations with eight requests in the unchanged original order. Tracking first errors reveals how the failure set expands and how many initial successes survive. Every request retains the full candidate menu.

The test reveals no general Jev advantage in preserving correct choices. Jev’s accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27.3–28.5%, with first failures continuing into the final presentation (Figure 1). Four LLMs preserve more initial successes, including on questions every model initially answers correctly. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash have lower pooled retention, preventing a universal ranking of model families. The central finding is that Jev’s structured decision formulation does not by itself protect answers the model can already get right.

Fixed-order repetition exposes a second distinction: repeatability does not ensure robustness to reordering. Both Jev versions repeat choices more consistently than all six LLMs, but lose substantially more initial successes under reordering than under repetition at the same call budget. The twelve Jev reproductions make this gap especially clear: 91.9–100% fixed-order agreement coexists with losses of 23.2–64.2% of initial successes under reordering (Figure 2).

The remaining analyses ask where correct choices are most fragile and whether repeated answers can help recover them. Comparisons by task, difficulty, and menu size locate this vulnerability; voting and unanimity test whether the observed variation or agreement offers a remedy. MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond then examine the scope of the findings, showing that correct choices remain vulnerable where Jev achieves higher accuracy and with only four candidates. Together, these analyses distinguish average accuracy, fixed-order repeatability, and preservation of correct choices. The supporting survey in Appendices A–I organizes differences in representation, learning, and computation that controlled comparisons could isolate to explain the observed behavior.

2 Evaluation Setup

2.1 Datasets

Our primary evaluation uses a fixed collection of 1,700 test questions: 1,200 from SuperGPQA (M-A-P et al., 2025) and 500 from LEXam (Fan et al., 2026).22 2 Dataset releases: SuperGPQA and LEXam. The benchmarks cover graduate-level knowledge and legal examination questions. We weight questions equally, so pooled scores reflect this sample composition rather than an equal-weight average of benchmark scores.

SuperGPQA contributes questions with 4–10 options from its official evaluation release, balanced across easy, middle, and hard difficulty. LEXam contributes 125 test questions at each of 4, 8, 16, and 32 options. This collection supports analyses by difficulty, discipline, and candidate count. Candidate count varies with benchmark and question content, so these comparisons are descriptive.

Two further datasets test the scope of the findings. MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024) contributes 300 test questions, with 100 each at eight, nine, and ten options and 21–22 from each of fourteen subjects. GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2023) contributes all 198 questions, each with four options.33 3 Dataset releases: MMLU-Pro and GPQA, Diamond subset. We report these datasets separately to examine whether the vulnerability persists at higher Jev accuracy and with short candidate menus. The balanced MMLU-Pro sample does not estimate accuracy over the full benchmark distribution. All question sets remain fixed across models and presentations.

2.2 Models

The Jev--LLM comparison includes Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14, with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-sol, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash as generative LLM baselines.44 4 Model documentation: Jev, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash. Jev returns a choice through its native decision interface. The LLMs receive a serialized representation of the same question and candidate menu and return a selection. Their training, inference procedures, and interfaces are not matched.

The comparison with Jev reproductions includes AutoTrust-JEV-9B, AutoTrust-JEV-27B, AutoTrust-JEV-35B, AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1, AutoTrust-JEV-Gemma4-26B-A4B, StartLux-Decision-v1-0.8B, StartLux-Decision-v1-2B, StartLux-Decision-v1-4B, StartLux-Decision-v1-9B, StartLux-Decision-v1-27B, StartLux-Decision-v1-35B-A3B (Zhuang et al., 2026), and pplx-decider-v1.1-27b.55 5 Official model cards: AutoTrust-JEV-27B, AutoTrust-JEV-Gemma4-26B-A4B, and pplx-decider-v1.1-27b. We select the candidate with the highest native probability, without generating an answer or using deliberation. Both Jev versions serve as references, giving twenty unique models across the two comparisons. Every model is evaluated on all four datasets.

2.3 Eight Presentations of Each Question

Across all four datasets, each question is presented in its original candidate order, the reversed order, and six random permutations. All models receive the same permutation for a given question. Each candidate’s identifier moves with its content, preserving their association, while the question and state remain unchanged. Every request retains the full menu. These are repeated measurements of fixed questions. In the primary collection, the first random permutation differs from the original, and each subsequent random permutation differs from all preceding permutations. MMLU-Pro has eight distinct orders per question, while GPQA Diamond has seven or eight.

The intervention changes the order of candidate entries without independently manipulating identifiers or rewriting answers. The original presentation provides a reference for trajectories; it is not assumed to be the least biased order. Requests are independent: later presentations do not include earlier model answers.

We request low reasoning effort for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, GPT-6.1-sol, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash, and use adaptive thinking with low effort for Claude Sonnet 5.5. Returned keys are mapped back to the original candidates. Moving a candidate to a different position does not count as a changed decision if the model selects the same candidate.

2.4 Repeated Requests in the Original Order

The original-order repetition study holds candidate content, identifiers, and order fixed across eight independent requests for every model: the original presentation and seven further requests. Following the distinction between repetition stability and position consistency in Shi et al. (2025), this condition measures fixed-order repeatability through same-candidate agreement across requests.

For each comparison, we contrast eight original-order presentations with eight reordered presentations: the original, reversal, and six random permutations. The two conditions share the original request and use the same questions. We compare changed-choice rates, loss of initial successes, mean accuracy, and plurality gains. Sensitivity analyses on the primary collection compare the first three original-order requests with the original and every pair of the seven non-original presentations, and remove the shared original request to compare two further repeats with reversal and the first permutation.

Same-candidate agreement requires selecting the same candidate in every request so far. A changed choice involves at least two distinct candidates. The same-wrong rate counts questions receiving the same wrong candidate throughout. Loss of initial successes is the fraction of first-request successes that become incorrect at least once. Pointwise 95% intervals use 2,000 benchmark-stratified bootstrap resamples of source groups, jointly preserving models and conditions; differences use paired draws.

2.5 Separating Scores, Correctness, and Error Identity

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} denote the evaluated collection or subgroup. For question x∈𝒬x\in\mathcal{Q}, let 𝒜x\mathcal{A}_{x} be its candidate set, yxy_{x} its correct candidate, and y^x,t\widehat{y}_{x,t} the model’s answer in presentation t∈{1,…,8}t\in\{1,\ldots,8\}. Accuracy is the proportion of questions answered correctly in each presentation. For a given model, define

Ct={x∈𝒬:y^x,t=yx},Rt=|⋂s=1tCs||C1|.C_{t}=\{x\in\mathcal{Q}:\widehat{y}_{x,t}=y_{x}\},\qquad R_{t}=\frac{|\bigcap_{s=1}^{t}C_{s}|}{|C_{1}|}. (1)

We call RtR_{t} retention: the fraction of initially correct questions that remain correct in every presentation through tt. Its complement, 1−Rt1-R_{t}, is the loss of initial successes. A question that becomes wrong and later recovers no longer belongs to the retained set. Retention therefore measures continued correctness, rather than overlap with the correct set in the latest presentation alone. Both quantities are undefined when there are no initial successes.

Within the Jev–LLM comparison, we additionally restrict 𝒬\mathcal{Q} to questions answered correctly by all eight models in the original presentation. Each model’s retention then uses this same denominator. We report paired differences with 2,000 bootstrap resamples of source groups within each benchmark, jointly preserving all models and rounds. This analysis is conditional on the observed shared initial-correct set; it removes differences in which questions enter the comparison, without matching model capability or training.

To measure how many questions have failed, define the cumulative failed set and the number of first failures in presentation tt as

Ft=⋃s=1t(𝒬∖Cs),Bt=|Ft|,Nt=|Ft∖Ft−1|,F_{t}=\bigcup_{s=1}^{t}(\mathcal{Q}\setminus C_{s}),\qquad B_{t}=|F_{t}|,\qquad N_{t}=|F_{t}\setminus F_{t-1}|, (2)

with F0=∅F_{0}=\varnothing. Each question enters FtF_{t} once, at its first incorrect outcome. Later mistakes on that question add nothing to NtN_{t}, even if the selected wrong candidate changes. Figure 1(c) reports BtB_{t}. The cumulative count is bounded by the number of questions, and Bt−B1=|C1|(1−Rt)B_{t}-B_{1}=|C_{1}|(1-R_{t}) links additional failures to the loss of initial successes.

Separately, accuracy discards changes in the identity of an incorrect answer. To track wrong-option diversity, we count distinct question–wrong-option pairs through presentation tt:

Ut=|⋃s=1t{(x,a):x∈𝒬,a∈𝒜x∖{yx},y^x,s=a}|.U_{t}=\left|\bigcup_{s=1}^{t}\{(x,a):x\in\mathcal{Q},\ a\in\mathcal{A}_{x}\setminus\{y_{x}\},\ \widehat{y}_{x,s}=a\}\right|. (3)

Selecting the same wrong option again on the same question adds nothing to UtU_{t}; selecting another wrong option adds one. Consequently, UtU_{t} may exceed the number of questions ever answered incorrectly. It is nondecreasing by construction. The empirical quantities of interest are how many new pairs each presentation adds and how often a single question receives multiple distinct wrong answers.

To separate question coverage from wrong-option diversity, let kx,tk_{x,t} be the number of distinct wrong options selected for question xx through presentation tt, and let Wt=|{x∈𝒬:kx,t>0}|W_{t}=|\{x\in\mathcal{Q}:k_{x,t}>0\}|. Then

Ut=Wt+Dt,Dt=∑x∈𝒬max⁡(kx,t−1,0).U_{t}=W_{t}+D_{t},\qquad D_{t}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{Q}}\max(k_{x,t}-1,0). (4)

Each question contributes its first observed wrong candidate to WtW_{t} and any additional distinct wrong candidates to DtD_{t}. Since D1=0D_{1}=0, growth decomposes as Ut−U1=(Wt−W1)+DtU_{t}-U_{1}=(W_{t}-W_{1})+D_{t}.

2.6 Stratification and Uncertainty

The pooled collection supports complementary views of stability. Within each full subgroup 𝒬g\mathcal{Q}_{g}, we report accuracy averaged over the eight presentations, the percentage of questions with at least two distinct selected candidates, loss of initially correct questions (100​(1−R8)100(1-R_{8})), and extra wrong pairs per 100 questions (100​D8/|𝒬g|100D_{8}/|\mathcal{Q}_{g}|). Changed choices split into questions selecting both the correct candidate and an actual wrong candidate, and questions selecting multiple wrong candidates without ever selecting the correct one. These disjoint groups sum to the changed-choice rate. For the option-count comparison, we also report newly failed questions per 100 questions, 100​(B8−B1)/|𝒬g|100(B_{8}-B_{1})/|\mathcal{Q}_{g}|. This measures first failures after the original presentation across the full subgroup, whereas 100​(1−R8)100(1-R_{8}) measures loss conditional on initial success.

We use the source metadata to partition SuperGPQA into easy, middle, and hard questions (400 each) and broad disciplines. We also examine difficulty within the ten-option subset: 264 easy, 258 middle, and 209 hard questions. LEXam groups use option count. Both model comparisons include every observed menu size, from four to 32 options; these groups differ in benchmark composition as well as content. We pool the five SuperGPQA disciplines with fewer than 30 sampled questions for visualization. Difficulty labels are available only for SuperGPQA; we do not assign them to the other benchmarks.

Error bars show pointwise 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 bootstrap samples. We resample source groups within each benchmark, keeping all presentations and models together within each resampled group. We omit intervals for groups with fewer than 20 questions or eight independent units. These exploratory intervals summarize sampling variation within the observed groups, without simultaneous coverage or a causal interpretation of differences between groups.

2.7 Voting and Agreement Across Presentations

We use the eight selections to examine whether agreement provides useful evidence of correctness. Plurality voting selects the most frequently chosen candidate, without requiring an absolute majority. For ties, we report expected correctness under a uniform draw among the tied candidates. This rule favors neither the original presentation nor the gold answer. We compare voting with mean single-presentation accuracy on 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The difference measures the gain from combining eight answers rather than using one of the eight with equal probability.

Unanimous coverage is the fraction of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} receiving the same candidate selection in all eight presentations. Accuracy within this subset measures how reliably unanimous answers are correct. We report these quantities together because higher conditional accuracy can come at the cost of answering fewer questions. The pooled bootstrap resamples source groups within each benchmark, preserving all models and presentations together. Voting under original-order repetition also uses eight calls for every model (Section 2.4).

3 Does Jev Resist Changes in Option Order?

The central question concerns the survival of correct choices, not just the stability of a score. We first trace the failures hidden by aggregate accuracy, then compare their extent with LLM baselines and with fixed-order repetition.

3.1 What Stable Accuracy Conceals

All eight models in the Jev–LLM comparison maintain similar accuracy across presentations despite substantial differences in their overall performance. Jev scores near 50%, spanning only 1.47 percentage points for version 1.13 and 1.53 for version 1.14. The LLMs score approximately 56–72%, with similarly narrow ranges of 1.12–2.59 points (Figure 1(a)).

Between two presentations, let nC​Wn_{CW} count correct-to-incorrect transitions, nW​Cn_{WC} incorrect-to-correct transitions, and nWW′n_{WW\prime} transitions between two distinct wrong candidates. Over 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, the accuracy change and combined transition rate are

Δ​Acc𝒬=nW​C−nC​W|𝒬|,T=nC​W+nW​C+nWW′|𝒬|.\Delta\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\frac{n_{WC}-n_{CW}}{|\mathcal{Q}|},\qquad T=\frac{n_{CW}+n_{WC}+n_{WW\prime}}{|\mathcal{Q}|}. (5)

Losses and recoveries offset each other in accuracy but add in the transition rate. Switches between wrong candidates affect only the latter, exposing further variation hidden by a stable score.

Jev 1.14 illustrates this cancellation under reversal (Figure 3): 113 correct answers become incorrect and 120 incorrect answers become correct, yielding a net gain of seven. Another 176 choices move between wrong candidates, bringing the total to 409 transitions. GPT-6.1-sol gains six correct answers despite 170 transitions: 56 losses, 62 recoveries, and 52 wrong-to-wrong switches. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash have 459 and 620 transitions for net gains of only 19 and 26. Similar score changes thus conceal different amounts of turnover, including failures on questions each model could previously answer.

The same cancellation occurs in Jev reproductions (Figure 4). AutoTrust-JEV-9B loses 167 correct answers and recovers 170, while another 377 choices switch between wrong candidates. Its 714 transitions yield a net gain of three correct answers. Across all eight presentations, the twelve Jev reproductions’ accuracy ranges are only 1.12–2.18 points (Figure 2(a)). Stable aggregate performance therefore offers little evidence that individual decisions are preserved.

3.2 First Failures Continue Beyond the Initial Presentations

Obs. 1. Jev’s stable accuracy hides an expanding set of failed questions.

Jev 1.13 fails on 845 questions in the original presentation and on 1,076 across all eight, while Jev 1.14 rises from 840 to 1,079 (Figure 1(c)). The additional 231 and 239 questions expand the observed failure sets by 27.3% and 28.5%, despite the narrow accuracy ranges. The LLMs also expose new failures, ranging from 135 for GPT-6.1-sol to 451 for GLM-5.3-Flash, with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, and GLM-5.3-Flash exceeding Jev. Absolute additions alone do not establish a robustness ranking, however, because models begin with different numbers of correct answers available to lose.

First failures continue well beyond the initial reversal. Reversal exposes 105 and 113 for the two Jev versions; the eighth presentation still reveals eleven and eight questions answered correctly in all seven preceding presentations. Cumulative counts are nondecreasing by definition. The empirical finding is the scale of the expansion and the continued loss of questions that have already survived several orders.

All twelve Jev reproductions likewise expose first failures in the eighth presentation, adding 3–14 per model (Figure 2(c)). Even AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1, which has comparatively favorable retention, expands from 887 failed questions in the original order to 1,076 across the sequence, with 11 first failures in the final presentation.

3.3 Persistence on Shared Initial Successes

Obs. 2. Jev’s retention disadvantage persists against four LLMs on shared initial successes.

To compare the loss of correct choices across models, retention normalizes first-failure expansion by the number of initial successes: B8−B1=|C1|(1−R8)B_{8}-B_{1}=|C_{1}|(1-R_{8}). Across all eight presentations, Jev retains 72.2–73.0% of its initially correct answers, compared with 75.7–88.9% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash, 64.1% for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, and 52.0% for GLM-5.3-Flash (Figure 1(d)). Equivalently, 27.0–27.8% of Jev’s initial successes fail at least once. Four LLMs preserve a larger fraction of initial successes than Jev, while the lower retention of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash rules out a blanket Jev–LLM ranking.

This comparison could be affected by which questions each model answers correctly in the first place. We therefore repeat it on the 487 shared initial successes, requiring every model to begin with a correct answer to every included question. Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 retain 85.0% and 84.4%, respectively. Retention reaches 92.6% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, 96.1% for Claude Sonnet 5.5, 98.4% for GPT-6.1-sol, and 97.7% for Gemini 3.8 Flash. GPT-6.1-sol has paired advantages of 13.3 percentage points over Jev 1.13 (95% interval 9.9–16.6) and 14.0 over Jev 1.14 (10.5–17.2). The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash intervals also exclude zero. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next retains 84.8%, with differences of −0.2-0.2 points from Jev 1.13 (−4.5-4.5–3.7) and 0.4 from Jev 1.14 (−3.9-3.9–4.5); neither interval establishes a difference. GLM-5.3-Flash retains only 69.6%, below both Jev versions, with both paired intervals excluding zero.

Matching initial successes therefore preserves Jev’s disadvantage relative to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash, while bringing Qwen3.8-Flash-Next close to Jev and leaving GLM-5.3-Flash below it. This comparison controls which questions enter the calculation, without matching model capability, training, or variation under repeated requests.

Retention also varies widely among Jev reproductions. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 loses 23.2% of initial successes, below the Jev reference losses of 27.0% and 27.8%. The other eleven reproductions lose 30.0–64.2%, including 30.0% for pplx-decider-v1.1-27b and 49.5% for AutoTrust-JEV-Gemma4-26B-A4B. Native candidate prediction thus supports implementations on both sides of the Jev results. These rates condition on each model’s own initial successes, so their spread also reflects differences in the questions each model initially answers correctly.

3.4 Repeatability Under a Fixed Order

Obs. 3. Jev’s repeatability under a fixed order does not imply robustness to reordering.

The preceding comparisons leave open how much variation occurs even when the order stays fixed. Eight original-order requests provide this reference (Figure 1(b)). Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 achieve 84.9% and 83.6% same-candidate agreement, exceeding all six LLMs. GPT-6.1-sol reaches 82.0% and Gemini 3.8 Flash 83.0%, while GLM-5.3-Flash falls to 42.1% even without a menu change. The models thus differ substantially in their tendency to change an answer with the menu held fixed.

High repeatability also includes repeated mistakes (Figure 5). Across eight original-order requests, 37.5–39.3% of all questions receive the same wrong Jev answer throughout, and accuracy among its unanimous answers is only 53.7–55.1%. A stable choice therefore provides limited assurance of correctness.

The Jev reproductions combine even higher agreement with frequent repeated errors (Figure 6). They agree on 91.9–100% of all questions across eight requests, yet 48.5–72.2% receive the same wrong answer throughout. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 repeats the same candidate on every question; pplx-decider-v1.1-27b reaches 97.7% agreement. Repeatedly selecting the argmax of native candidate probabilities can therefore produce highly stable errors.

At an equal eight-call budget, Jev varies substantially more under reordering than under original-order repetition (Figure 7). Its changed-choice rate is 25.8 percentage points higher for version 1.13 (95% interval 23.7–28.1) and 25.9 higher for version 1.14 (23.6–28.2), compared with differences of 2.1–7.2 across the six LLMs. This gap also extends to successful decisions. Jev loses 8.8–9.2% of its initial successes under repetition and 27.0–27.8% under reordering, with paired differences of 17.8 points (15.2–20.5) and 19.0 points (16.1–22.0), while mean accuracy differs by less than half a point. By contrast, GLM-5.3-Flash already loses 42.1% under original-order repetition, with a further 5.9-point difference under reordering. Variation under repetition and additional variation under reordering are distinct failure patterns.

For the Jev reproductions, the repetition reference makes the contrast sharper: they lose only 0–1.3% of initial successes under repetition, compared with 23.2–64.2% under reordering (Figure 8). Their changed-choice rates are 36.3–68.5 percentage points higher under reordering, versus differences of 25.8 and 25.9 for the Jev references. Choices that are almost perfectly repeatable in a fixed order can thus remain fragile across orders.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next shows why the overall failure rate and the repetition–reordering gap answer different questions. Its changed-choice rate rises from 46.3% under repetition to 51.1% under reordering, an increase of 4.8 points compared with Jev’s 25.8–25.9. Its loss of initial successes rises by 3.6 points, from 32.3% to 35.9%. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next loses more successes than Jev under reordering, but much of its variability is already present with the menu fixed.

Shorter sequences give the same qualitative result. Combining the original with each of the 21 pairs of non-original presentations yields a three-call comparison against three original-order requests. On the full question set, Jev’s excess changed-choice rate is 18.5–21.3 points for version 1.13 and 19.7–21.7 for version 1.14, versus 0.6–6.6 across the LLMs. Removing the shared original request also retains a 12.6–13.5-point excess for Jev. The large repetition–reordering gap is therefore not specific to using all eight presentations or including their shared initial response.

3.5 Errors Extend Beyond a Single Distractor

First-failure counts do not distinguish a persistent distractor from several distinct wrong answers on the same question. We therefore examine distinct question–wrong-option pairs, retaining selections after a question’s first error.

Obs. 4. Jev’s errors often extend beyond one distractor per question.

If every question with an observed wrong answer had one fixed distractor, wrong-pair growth would reflect only additional questions selecting a wrong candidate. Jev 1.14 illustrates why this description is incomplete. Its original presentation produces 840 wrong pairs, one for each incorrectly answered question. After eight presentations, 1,079 questions have failed at least once, but the model has selected 1,676 distinct wrong pairs. The 836 additional pairs comprise 239 newly affected questions and 597 extra wrong candidates beyond the first per affected question. The latter component includes both initially failed questions and questions that first fail later and then receive another wrong answer.

Equation 4 separates these two sources for every model (Figure 9). Extra wrong candidates account for 70.2–71.4% of Jev’s pair growth, compared with 67.2% for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 72.4% for GLM-5.3-Flash, and 52.9–60.6% for the other four LLMs. For example, GPT-6.1-sol’s increase from 485 to 771 pairs comprises 133 additional questions with an observed wrong candidate and 153 extra wrong candidates. Most of Jev’s pair growth thus reflects additional ways to fail on affected questions, beyond the spread of failures counted in Obs. 3.2.

Extra wrong candidates account for 70.8–89.5% of wrong-pair growth in the twelve Jev reproductions, from AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 to StartLux-Decision-v1-0.8B (Figure 10). High fixed-order agreement can thus coexist with several distinct wrong answers to the same question under reordering.

Jev’s distinct wrong-pair count increases by 91.8–99.5%, far more than its 27.3–28.5% increase in failed questions. This is not the largest relative pair growth: the LLM increases range from 59.0% for GPT-6.1-sol to 220.1% for GLM-5.3-Flash, with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next also exceeding Jev. The distinction is between spreading failure to more questions and exposing more ways to fail on a question.

Multiple distractors are selected on 394–419 questions for Jev, below Qwen3.8-Flash-Next’s 451 and GLM-5.3-Flash’s 663, and above the 117–261 for the other four LLMs. Their contribution persists late in the sequence. Of the 49 and 63 new wrong pairs in Jev’s final presentation, 38 and 55 select a different wrong candidate on a previously affected question, accounting for 77.6% and 87.3% of the additions. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 show a similar pattern, with shares of 76.8% and 78.6%. Late error discovery therefore mainly broadens the observed ways to fail within affected questions, even as a smaller number of previously successful questions fail for the first time.

The expansion is not specific to choosing the original or final presentation as a reference. Relative to the mean wrong-pair count of a single presentation, the full union is 90.5–97.6% larger for Jev and 60.4–225.9% larger for the LLMs. Averaging over all eight ways to omit one presentation leaves 51.6–56.9 unseen pairs for Jev, versus 20.5–147.9 for the LLMs. These comparisons characterize the diversity of observed errors without predicting saturation under further evaluation. Because every request retains the full menu, they also leave open how the model would respond if a wrong candidate were removed.

4 How Does Jev’s Order Robustness Vary Across Tasks?

The pooled results establish that Jev’s stable score conceals lost successes. We now ask how broadly this pattern holds across benchmarks, difficulty levels, topics, and menu sizes. Each profile separates changed choices from lost initial successes, since a model can appear stable by remaining wrong. These subgroup comparisons locate vulnerability without isolating its causes.

4.1 Comparisons Across Benchmarks

Obs. 5. Jev’s relative stability depends on the task and the LLM comparator.

The ordering of models by stability can change across benchmarks (Figure 11). On LEXam, Jev changes 39.8–42.0% of choices, below DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017’s 48.0%, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next’s 62.8%, and GLM-5.3-Flash’s 77.0%, but above GPT-6.1-sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5.5. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 instead changes fewer choices than either Jev version on SuperGPQA. GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash remain more stable than Jev on both benchmarks, while Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash remain less stable. Jev’s relative position therefore depends on both the task and the comparator.

AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 changes fewer choices than either Jev version on both primary benchmarks, but this does not translate into uniformly better retention (Figure 12). On LEXam, its loss of 20.5% lies between Jev 1.13’s 21.7% and Jev 1.14’s 17.9%, despite changing fewer choices than both. The distinction between preserving candidate identity and preserving correct answers therefore matters even among Jev-style models.

The changed choices themselves also differ in whether they ever reach a correct answer. Over half of Jev’s LEXam questions with changed choices remain wrong in every presentation. These always-wrong switches account for 21.4–21.6% of all LEXam questions, compared with 5.2–20.6% for the LLMs. Such trajectories contain no correct answer for voting to recover, linking the stability analysis to the aggregation results in Section 5.

4.2 Difficulty and the Persistence of Correct Answers

Obs. 6. Jev loses over half its initial successes on hard SuperGPQA questions.

Hard questions challenge Jev beyond lowering its accuracy. Even conditional on an initially correct answer, 53.9–54.6% later become wrong, compared with 14.1–36.2% for five LLMs and 59.5% for GLM-5.3-Flash (Figure 13). An initial Jev success on these questions is therefore more often lost than preserved across all eight presentations. Jev’s overall changed-choice rate also rises from 27.5–31.0% on easy questions to 60.8–62.5% on hard questions. Every LLM shows a smaller increase, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next’s rate decreases. For Jev, harder questions expose both more frequent changes and a greater loss of initially correct answers.

The difficulty gradient extends across the twelve Jev reproductions (Figure 14). Every model changes more choices on hard than easy SuperGPQA questions, including within ten-option menus. On hard questions overall, loss of initial successes ranges from 36.8% for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 to 88.5% for StartLux-Decision-v1-4B. High fixed-order agreement thus does not protect a correct answer once the model confronts harder questions in a different order.

Menu size does not fully explain this gradient. Within ten-option questions, Jev’s changed-choice rate rises from 27.7–29.9% on easy questions to 65.1–67.0% on hard questions; every LLM shows a smaller increase (Figure 13(d)). Question content and subject composition still differ, so this comparison does not isolate difficulty itself.

Correct-answer retention shows that the vulnerability is present even on easy questions (Figure 15). Within ten-option groups, Jev loses 15.7–20.1% of initial successes on easy questions, 27.7% on middle questions, and 50.0–53.4% on hard questions. Across all 731 ten-option questions, the loss is 28.0–29.5%, while each version’s accuracy varies by only 2.05 percentage points. Hard questions amplify the discrepancy between stable accuracy and fragile successes; they are not necessary for it to appear.

The same ten-option analysis separates the Jev reproductions (Figure 16). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 loses 18.2% of initial successes on easy questions and 44.9% on hard questions. The other eleven lose 66.2–93.3% on hard questions, compared with 50.0–53.4% for the Jev references in this comparison. A common candidate count therefore leaves substantial differences both across difficulty groups and within the Jev-style family.

Subject profiles help locate this difficulty gradient (Figure 17). Engineering and science contain much of Jev’s instability and many of the hard questions: 163 of 399 engineering questions and 142 of 321 science questions are hard, compared with nine of 93 in literature and arts. Their higher changed-choice rates are consistent with the difficulty result, without identifying an independent subject effect. Separating switches that include the correct candidate from always-wrong switches also reveals which variation includes an answer that aggregation could recover.

Subject profiles also qualify the relatively favorable pooled result for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 (Figure 18). It changes 43.9% of choices in engineering and 44.2% in science. Always-wrong switches account for 15.8% and 18.4% of all questions in those disciplines, respectively. Thus, its residual instability includes both lost or recovered correct answers and variation that never reaches the correct answer; the latter cannot be repaired by voting over the recorded choices.

4.3 Locating Instability Within Legal Tasks

LEXam reveals substantial heterogeneity across menu sizes. All eight models in the Jev–LLM comparison have lower accuracy and more changed choices in the 32-option group than in the four-option group (Figure 19). Jev’s changed-choice rates rise from 20.8–21.6% in the four-option group to 68.0–73.6% in the 32-option group. Both Jev versions exceed DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017’s 64.8% in the latter group, reversing their favorable comparison on LEXam overall. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash vary even more, changing 87.2% and 97.6% of choices. The same group yields 85.6–97.6 extra wrong pairs per 100 questions for Jev, compared with 162.4 for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and 237.6 for GLM-5.3-Flash. Larger menus thus identify a particularly unstable portion of this collection, with wrong-option diversity extending well beyond Jev. The groups contain different questions, however, and do not isolate the effect of adding distractors to a fixed question.

Every reproduction changes more choices at 16 options than at eight, and more at eight than at four (Figure 20). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 rises from 14.4% to 33.6% between four and 16 options, then reaches 55.2% at 32. Across four to 32 options, pplx-decider-v1.1-27b rises from 11.2% to 76.0%; AutoTrust-JEV-35B reaches 92.0% in the 32-option group.

4.4 Option Count and Continued Failure Discovery

The LEXam profiles raise a broader question: is the loss of correct choices concentrated in long menus? Across the primary collection, the loss persists on both sides of an eight-option threshold (Figure 21). Jev loses 22.2–24.1% of its initially correct answers on questions with fewer than eight options and 28.8–29.2% on questions with at least eight. The comparison with LLMs also varies across these groups. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 loses 25.8% and 23.8%, respectively: slightly more than either Jev version in the smaller-menu group, but less than both in the larger-menu group. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next loses 36.9% and 35.5%, exceeding both Jev versions in each group. These differences qualify pooled comparisons without isolating an effect of menu size.

Jev reproductions also lose initial successes in both groups (Figure 22). Losses range from 17.8–51.9% below eight options and 25.3–71.6% at eight or more. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 has lower loss than either Jev version in both groups. The other eleven reproductions lose a larger fraction of their initial successes than either Jev version in the larger-menu group, showing that the vulnerability extends across the evaluated implementations.

The full option-count profile qualifies the LEXam trend (Figure 23). Jev’s changed-choice rate and loss of initial successes fluctuate across the four- to ten-option groups rather than increasing steadily with menu size. Composition matters: all ten-option questions are from SuperGPQA, while all 16- and 32-option questions are from LEXam. The profile identifies vulnerable groups without estimating what would happen if distractors were added to the same question.

The pooled profile of Jev reproductions similarly prevents a simple ranking by menu size (Figure 24). AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 loses 25.6% of initial successes on ten-option questions and 22.6% on 16-option questions, although its LEXam-only turnover increases across menu sizes. These groups differ in both benchmark and question content.

Small menus do not make repeated reordering uninformative. A four-option question has 4!=244!=24 full permutations, so eight presentations need not repeat the same menu order. In the four-option group, 199 of 203 questions have eight distinct observed orders and the other four have seven. Jev 1.13’s cumulative failed-question count rises from 83 to 103, and Jev 1.14’s from 80 to 100. Presentations five through eight still expose five and two first failures, respectively. Counting only the first occurrence of each full permutation leaves both Jev failure trajectories unchanged. These distinct full orders need not place the correct answer in distinct positions. The curves measure robustness across the sampled menu orders, without assuming a new correct-answer position on every presentation.

The number of new failures must also be read alongside the pool of initial successes. On 32-option questions, Jev loses 44.0–66.7% of initial successes, but this amounts to only 8.8–12.8 newly failed questions per 100. The ten-option rates are 28.0–29.5% and 15.5–16.4 per 100. Low initial accuracy leaves fewer successes available to fail, so a smaller cumulative increase can accompany greater conditional fragility. Both measures are needed to avoid mistaking a small remaining pool of correct answers for robustness.

5 Can Aggregating Reordered Choices Correct Jev’s Errors?

The same repeated answers that expose failures might also help correct them. Plurality voting could recover a correct answer that appears across several orders, while unanimity could identify a more reliable subset. We test both possibilities, asking whether variation supplies useful correction and whether agreement warrants confidence (Figure 25).

5.1 Voting Recovers Only Part of the Error

Combining eight reordered answers gives Jev only a modest accuracy gain: 0.96 percentage points for version 1.13 (95% interval 0.32–1.64) and 1.01 for version 1.14 (0.34–1.70). The reference is mean single-presentation accuracy, avoiding dependence on an unusually weak original round. LLM gains range from 0.46 points for GPT-6.1-sol to 5.63 for GLM-5.3-Flash, with positive lower bounds for all six intervals. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash gain 4.11 points (3.26–4.94) and 5.63 (4.67–6.55), respectively. Their lower pooled retention thus coexists with more effective correction through voting.

The trajectories help explain why correction is limited. Jev 1.14 gains only 0.30 points on LEXam (−0.65-0.65–1.28), where many changed choices remain wrong throughout. Such trajectories supply no correct vote; even when the correct answer appears, it must receive enough votes to defeat the alternatives. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash gain 3.32 points (1.87–4.86) and 4.73 (2.99–6.67) on LEXam, while the GPT-6.1-sol and Gemini 3.8 Flash intervals span zero. The usefulness of variation depends on which candidates are selected and how often, rather than on the amount of disagreement alone.

The eight-call comparison further limits the practical benefit of Jev’s variation. Voting gain, measured relative to each condition’s mean single-request accuracy, is only 0.79 points higher under reordering for Jev 1.13 (95% interval 0.10–1.47) and 1.00 higher for Jev 1.14 (0.24–1.76), alongside a roughly 26-point difference in changed-choice rates. The direct differences in plurality accuracy between conditions have intervals spanning zero for both versions. Thus, the greater variation under reordering accompanies a small additional voting gain relative to a single answer, without establishing higher final voting accuracy than original-order repetition.

Voting gains for Jev reproductions are also modest despite substantial turnover (Figure 26). They range from 0.74 points for AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 (95% interval 0.18–1.31) to 2.49 for StartLux-Decision-v1-35B-A3B (1.71–3.32), with positive lower bounds for all twelve models. Reordering provides some recoverable correct choices, but the gains remain small relative to the widespread changes it exposes.

5.2 Agreement and Persistent Error

Obs. 7. More than one third of unanimous Jev answers are wrong.

Unanimity raises Jev’s conditional accuracy but leaves substantial error among the retained answers. The two versions select the same candidate in all eight presentations on 57.7–59.1% of questions, with accuracy of 62.1–63.3% on this subset. Thus, 36.7–37.9% of unanimous answers are wrong. These persistent mistakes account for 21.2–22.4% of all questions, each receiving the same wrong Jev answer eight times. They survive even the strongest agreement requirement available in the recorded trajectories. Such mistakes are not, by themselves, evidence of order bias; they show why surviving the reordering test is insufficient to certify a correct decision.

The same unanimity rule retains more accurate answers for each LLM, although at different coverage. The retained LLM answers are 17.8–21.5% wrong, compared with Jev’s 36.7–37.9%. GPT-6.1-sol has the broadest coverage at 80.9%, with 78.5% conditional accuracy, while DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Gemini 3.8 Flash retain 63.5–76.5% of questions at 79.1–81.0% accuracy. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and GLM-5.3-Flash retain fewer questions than Jev, at 46.0% and 35.0% coverage, but reach 81.8% and 82.2% accuracy. Agreement improves conditional accuracy within each model, yet the surviving Jev decisions remain substantially less reliable at these observed operating points. Differences in base accuracy and coverage prevent this comparison from isolating the predictive value of agreement or establishing a ranking at matched coverage.

The Jev reproductions reinforce this limitation of unanimity. Their unanimous subsets reach only 30.2–66.3% accuracy, with coverage ranging from 24.1% to 63.7% of the full collection. AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 has the highest coverage, yet 42.4% of its unanimous answers are wrong; these persistent errors account for 27.0% of all 1,700 questions. Across the twelve models, 12.1–27.0% of questions receive the same wrong answer in every presentation. Even agreement across reordered menus therefore leaves a substantial set of errors undetected.

6 Does Higher Accuracy Protect Correct Choices?

The primary collection leaves open whether fragile successes mainly accompany Jev’s relatively low accuracy on those tasks. MMLU-Pro provides a setting where Jev answers most questions correctly, allowing us to examine whether those successes also survive reordering.

Obs. 8. Higher Jev accuracy does not eliminate the loss of initial successes.

Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 average 86.4% and 86.0% accuracy over the reordered presentations, with ranges of 3.7 and 3.3 percentage points (Figure 27(a)). Yet their cumulative failure sets grow from 35 to 58 and from 36 to 63 questions, respectively. The additional 23 and 27 failures represent 8.7% and 10.2% of initially correct answers, compared with losses of only 1.1% and 2.7% under original-order repetition. Each version first fails on two more questions in the final presentation. The loss is smaller than on the primary collection, but it persists even when Jev answers most questions correctly.

All twelve Jev reproductions repeat exactly the same candidate across eight original-order requests, yet lose 8.6–45.0% of initial successes under reordering (Figure 28). Thus, the separation between repeatability and preservation of correct choices persists on a different benchmark. As in the primary collection, the comparison describes the evaluated systems without isolating an architectural cause.

Jev’s unanimous answers are more accurate here than on the primary collection, but agreement still does not certify correctness. They cover 88.3% and 86.0% of questions and reach 91.3% and 91.9% accuracy (Figure 27(d)); 8.7% and 8.1% of the retained answers are still wrong. Thus, both the loss under reordering and the reliability of agreement depend on the task collection. What transfers is the distinction among average accuracy, fixed-order repeatability, and the survival of individual correct decisions.

7 Does a Four-Option Menu Remove the Vulnerability?

MMLU-Pro extends the evidence to higher Jev accuracy, but its questions still have eight to ten options. GPQA Diamond tests whether the loss of initial successes persists on a separate benchmark where every question has only four options. Figures 29 and 30 use all 198 questions and the common eight-presentation protocol.

Obs. 9. Jev’s loss of correct choices is not confined to long candidate menus.

Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 average 76.6% and 72.6% accuracy, yet their cumulative failure sets grow from 52 to 76 and from 58 to 89 questions. Reordering loses 16.4% and 22.1% of their initial successes, compared with 4.1% and 7.1% under original-order repetition. All twelve Jev reproductions repeat their original choices perfectly but lose 23.7–66.7% of initial successes after reordering. The gap between repeatability and preservation of successful decisions therefore extends to four-option questions. It does not require the larger menus in the primary collection.

The observed loss of initial successes varies across the LLMs, from 3.3% for GPT-6.1-sol to 21.7% for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and 44.9% for GLM-5.3-Flash. These results do not establish a uniform family ranking. Repeated errors also need not select the same distractor. Jev accumulates 95 and 112 distinct wrong question–candidate pairs across its 76 and 89 failed questions. The reproductions accumulate 142–281 such pairs. Excluding the two questions with duplicate distractor text preserves the Jev repetition–reordering gap. Short menus therefore remain informative about the survival of correct choices, although comparisons across benchmarks do not isolate candidate count from content or difficulty.

8 Implications and Scope

What the Jev comparison establishes.

Our results provide no evidence of a general Jev advantage in preserving correct choices across option orders. Four LLMs retain more shared initial successes (Obs. 3.3), but Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, GLM-5.3-Flash, and the task-dependent comparisons rule out a universal ranking. The contribution beyond pairwise order-sensitivity studies (Lukassen et al., 2026) is to trace the cumulative consequences: which initial successes are lost, how widely failures spread, and whether further orders still reveal first failures. The magnitude and timing of that loss carry the evidence; monotonic growth of a cumulative set does not.

The Jev reproductions show that a shared decision interface can coexist with substantially different robustness. On the primary collection, AutoTrust-JEV-27B-v1.1 retains more initial successes than the Jev references, whereas the other eleven reproductions retain fewer. Their high fixed-order agreement does not predict this ordering. Explaining the differences requires isolating the choices in representation, learning, and computation that the shared interface leaves unspecified.

Reordering diagnoses failures that agreement may not repair.

A useful diagnostic need not be an effective correction. Reordering exposes lost successes and multiple wrong candidates, but voting yields only a small accuracy gain for Jev. Always-wrong trajectories contain no correct vote, and unanimous errors pass an agreement filter unchanged (Obs. 5.2). These persistent errors do not themselves demonstrate order bias; they limit agreement as a safeguard. Nor does observing several wrong candidates establish what would happen after one is removed. An adaptive masking study could compare removing the previously selected wrong candidate with removing a random distractor at matched menu sizes, separating targeted correction from the benefit of fewer choices.

Behavioral differences do not identify their mechanism.

Original-order repetition characterizes variation without changing the menu. Its comparison with reordering describes behavioral differences without isolating a causal order effect. Candidate identifiers travel with their content while entry order changes, leaving the source of presentation sensitivity unresolved. Prior work distinguishes identifier preferences from position and context effects (Azizi et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2024); our experiment neither separates these components nor establishes how a proprietary interface represents them.

Training, inference, and interface also differ across models, precluding a causal claim about decision heads or generation. The literature offers starting points for controlled comparisons: frozen LLM readouts keep the backbone fixed (Li and Wagle, 2026), and serialization interventions keep weights fixed (Azizi et al., 2026). Further comparisons could vary decision-specific adaptation or candidate interaction separately. The supporting survey organizes these distinctions alongside supervision, gradient paths, and execution. The present findings concern observed selections, not a recovered account of Jev’s proprietary mechanism.

The task mixture limits generalization.

The results cover fixed task collections and eight presentations. Domain, language, difficulty, and candidate count vary together, while subgroup intervals are exploratory and do not adjust for multiple comparisons. MMLU-Pro and GPQA Diamond broaden the evidence, but differences in loss magnitude show its dependence on the collection. Continued first failures establish persistence within the observed sequence without predicting growth under further requests.

9 Related Work

Selection bias and its sources.

Early work on contextual calibration shows that language models carry answer preferences that can destabilize few-shot predictions as prompts and demonstrations change (Zhao et al., 2021). Option reordering provides a more direct test when question and answer content are held fixed (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024). Position and identifier effects must nevertheless be distinguished. Zheng et al. (2024) identify preferences for option-ID tokens as a major source of multiple-choice selection bias, while FairEval and MT-Bench document response-order effects in pairwise judgments (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023). In their study of many-shot evaluation, Song et al. (2025) likewise find that changing response order or the symbols assigned to responses alters GPT-4o’s pairwise judgments; they combine evaluations across both transformations to mitigate these biases. Shi et al. (2025) further separate repetition stability, position consistency, and preference fairness. Our candidate identifiers move with their content, so the present experiment measures behavior across reordered menus without independently identifying these sources.

Mitigation through calibration, training, and reasoning.

Contextual calibration and PriDe estimate answer priors to reduce bias (Zhao et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024). CalibraEval extends label-free calibration to LLM judges through an order-preserving transformation of prediction distributions (Li et al., 2024). Training offers another route. Strengthened symbol binding improves the association between an option and its identifier (Xue et al., 2024), while permutation-aware GRPO rewards consistency across rearrangements of the same instance (Zheng et al., 2026). Recent work also combines a probability-based permutation metric with LoRA fine-tuning and efficient aggregation (Guda et al., 2025). These interventions show that selection bias is responsive to both training and inference procedures. Evidence of reduced position bias in reasoning models on multi-document question answering further motivates comparison with current LLMs (Li et al., 2026). We evaluate the deployed systems without applying an additional debiasing method to any of them.

Jev-style modeling and selection bias.

Methods for reproducing Jev-style decisions differ in candidate representation, readout, and learning. LLM-as-Jev can even extract candidate probabilities from frozen causal LLMs (Li and Wagle, 2026), so the decision formulation alone does not identify an architectural or training intervention. Lukassen et al. (2026) compare eight typed decision models with seven LLM judges in pairwise evaluations, finding sensitivity to swapping two responses despite strong repeatability. Azizi et al. (2026) trace option-label effects to serialization in several public Jev-style implementations through interventions with weights fixed. These studies already establish that typed decisions need not be unbiased. We examine the cumulative consequences in multiple-choice tasks with four to 32 candidates. Repeated permutations reveal how widely failures spread, how much initial success survives, and whether voting or agreement can recover reliable decisions. Fixed-order repetition and contemporary LLM baselines place those losses in context.

Consistency, correctness, and aggregation.

MT-Bench cautions that a judge can be consistently wrong (Zheng et al., 2023). GRP evaluates each response pair in both orders and counts it as correct only when both judgments match the gold preference (Song et al., 2026). Asking for the worse response improves this joint criterion, without isolating gains in order agreement from gains in per-trial correctness. Ok et al. (2026) distinguish answer flipping from positional skew and show that aggregation can reduce flipping partly by stabilizing an incorrect answer. Their decomposition applies under balanced rotations, which our sampled permutations do not enforce. Likewise, the permutation metric of Guda et al. (2025) measures changes in candidate probabilities, whereas our analysis follows returned selections. We distinguish variation under repeated requests from variation under reordered menus, then test whether voting corrects errors and whether agreement identifies correct answers for Jev and the LLM baselines.

10 Conclusion

A simple reordering test reveals a limitation of Jev-style System One models: stable accuracy and repeatable choices can conceal the loss of successful decisions. Across eight presentations of the primary collection, the two Jev versions’ failure sets expand by 27.3–28.5% while accuracy remains nearly unchanged. Reordering loses substantially more initial successes than fixed-order repetition, a gap also observed in highly repeatable Jev reproductions. The LLM comparison establishes no general Jev advantage, and the vulnerability persists at higher accuracy and with short menus. Voting offers limited correction for Jev, and unanimous errors remain undetected by agreement alone. The central requirement is to evaluate whether individual correct choices survive equivalent presentations. Establishing which design choices improve that survival requires controlled comparisons beyond the shared interface.
