A Survey of Jev-Style System One Models

Appendix A Survey Overview

The main study shows that Jev’s stable accuracy and high fixed-order agreement can coexist with substantial losses of correct choices under reordering. It leaves the responsible mechanisms unresolved. Jev-style methods share a candidate-distribution interface while differing in representation, learning, computation, and downstream use. This survey organizes those differences to identify what a controlled test of structural robustness would need to vary.

A candidate distribution can be extracted from a frozen language model or learned from labels, contrastive pairs, reasoning teachers, and policy rewards (Geuter et al., 2026; Li and Wagle, 2026; Duan et al., 2026; Gao and Wang, 2026). A direct response can also arise from intermediate exits, recurrent latent processing, or conditional reasoning (Panchal, 2026; Gan et al., 2026; Zhuang et al., 2026). The output format therefore does not specify how a decision is learned or computed.

We organize the evidence around model construction, downstream workflows, and evaluation, building on prior distinctions among decision-model roles (Tang and Zheng, 2026; Ling et al., 2026a). Appendices C and D examine how distributions are learned and computed; Appendix E examines what they control. Appendix F connects local prediction quality to task outcomes, where local savings need not improve overall success (Ling et al., 2026b). Appendix G develops the resulting controlled comparisons.

Appendix B Decision Interfaces and Contribution Boundaries

B.1 The Decision Contract

A decision interface changes the contract between a model and its caller. Given a state ss, question qq, and finite candidate set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the model reports

pθ​(c∣s,q,𝒞),c∈𝒞.p_{\theta}(c\mid s,q,\mathcal{C}),\qquad c\in\mathcal{C}. (6)

Because the caller supplies candidates at inference, this contract extends beyond classification into a fixed training vocabulary. Choices, binary judgments, and ordinal scores can all expose such distributions. Constraining the response to the declared output space ensures its type; it does not ensure semantic correctness, calibration, or consistency across questions.

Official Jev combines this interface with a proprietary model and a service that reuses shared state across parallel questions. TypeSafe describes a new architecture and Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), but the public documentation available at the evidence cutoff does not disclose a reproducible architecture, training distribution, or exact objective.66 6 Official launch: https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev; machine-learning primer: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/machine-learning-primer. Consequently, public alternatives reproduce aspects of behavior or explore independently specified designs. They do not establish that Jev’s internal algorithm has been recovered.

Model version and service behavior are also distinct. Shared-state execution, candidate limits, scalar-score conventions, and calibration transformations can change behavior behind the same interface.77 7 Official model specifications: https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.

We cover publicly documented finite-candidate models, selected multimodal extensions, and downstream decision workflows available by October 19, 2026, identified through arXiv, citation tracing, official documentation, and linked releases. Appendix I summarizes additional implementations.

B.2 The Object of Contribution

A paper’s contribution depends on what its Jev call does (Table 1). AutoTrust uses Jev to obtain training targets for a replacement model; Jev-Mem uses it to control memory operations. An integration study may instead evaluate an existing workflow. These roles can overlap: CLM and FunDM each provide a model recipe and a coding-run selector, JEVal provides a benchmark and SII, and LAVOIR extends Laya while defining an information-acquisition policy.

Existing surveys already recognize distinct uses of typed decision models. Tang and Zheng (2026) discuss roles including controllers, judges, and replacements for individual steps, while Ling et al. (2026a) distinguish application domains from decision purposes in public repositories. We build on that distinction and focus on how specific model mechanisms connect to specific workflow operations.

Appendix C Constructing Decision Distributions

Candidate probabilities depend on the readout, the information shared among candidates, the supervision target, and the gradient estimator. These choices determine how order can enter the prediction and which interventions can change it. We examine each before turning to inference in Appendix D.

C.1 Decision Readout Before Specialized Training

Takeaway 1. A direct decision interface can expose a frozen model’s existing predictions.

A language model’s existing probabilities can be restricted and normalized over a candidate menu without updating its weights. This frozen readout provides a baseline for assessing what specialized adaptation adds, even when its predictions remain imperfect.

The simplest route reads an existing model’s candidate-token logits. The frozen baseline in Inner Jev renders alternatives with answer letters, disables thinking, and applies a softmax over the corresponding original language-model head rows (Geuter et al., 2026). Writing these logits as zkz_{k}, its calibrated readout is

pk=exp⁡(zk/T)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj/T).p_{k}=\frac{\exp(z_{k}/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_{j}/T)}. (7)

No model weights need change, although fitting TT still requires calibration data. SemIf and several community implementations use closely related answer-logit extraction. This route is an essential control for attributing improvements to specialized training: comparison against an LLM that must generate probability strings measures a different inference procedure.

LLM-as-Jev removes the restriction to a fixed pool of single-token labels without altering the architecture or tokenizer (Li and Wagle, 2026). A prompt ending in Best answer: [ assigns candidate kk the suffix k]. The closing bracket makes these suffixes prefix-free. For suffix tokens ck,1:mkc_{k,1:m_{k}}, it computes

sk=∑t=1mklog⁡pθ​(ck,t∣x,ck,<t),pk=esk∑jesj,s_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{m_{k}}\log p_{\theta}(c_{k,t}\mid x,c_{k,<t}),\qquad p_{k}=\frac{e^{s_{k}}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{j}}}, (8)

where xx contains the shared context and all alternatives. Prefix caching and parallel teacher-forced scoring make this inexpensive, but the paper describes generally one to three short forward steps after prefill. “No free-form answer generation” is therefore more accurate than a universal single-pass claim. The same framework can also inherit explicit thinking from its backbone.

C.2 Candidate Representations, Interaction, and Reuse

Takeaway 2. Reusable candidate representations can support set-dependent decisions.

Candidate representations can depend on the request, rival options, and serialization position. Caching constrains their computation but not how later layers combine them: reusable options can support set-dependent decisions, while request-conditioned options can remain isolated from rivals (Figure 32). Order invariance and sensitivity to meaningful set changes are therefore separate properties.

Independent scores with reusable candidate representations.

CLM independently encodes state–instruction and action inputs, then compares their projected representations. If these inputs and the temperature remain fixed, adding an alternative changes the softmax denominator but not the odds between two existing alternatives. MetaEncoder also uses a shared bi-encoder and contrastive training, but supports multimodal requests and updates the encoder (Cheng et al., 2026a). Its request-to-candidate InfoNCE is unidirectional, unlike CLM’s bidirectional objective. Moreover, its closed-set request template can include the alternatives, which are randomly dropped during training. Candidate features remain request-independent, but the request representation need not be independent of the set. Thus a bi-encoder label alone does not establish invariant pairwise odds.

Reusable candidates with set-dependent decisions.

Jeva independently encodes the request and each option, then refines only the request state against immutable option memory (Li and Wang, 2026). Candidate representations exclude the current request, their position, and other options, enabling reuse across requests. A compact decision stack nevertheless allows the final request state to depend on the entire option set. Shared scoring and symmetric aggregation are designed to make the resulting probability vector permutation-equivariant, while allowing the relative ranking of existing options to change when the set changes. Jeva further separates competition among options from coverage: for closed-set probabilities qiq_{i} and estimated coverage ρ\rho, the open-set output is pi=ρ​qip_{i}=\rho q_{i} with p∅=1−ρp_{\varnothing}=1-\rho. A diffuse qq expresses uncertainty among options; low ρ\rho expresses possible answer absence. Their empirical quality still depends on learning and evaluation.

Request-conditioned candidate blocks.

Candidate-independent block-causal attention offers a third design (Amit, 2026). A causal request prefix is shared; each candidate block attends to that prefix and its own tokens, but not to other candidate blocks. Reset positions and a shared local score head aim to remove serialization-order effects. Candidate states therefore depend on the request and cannot generally be cached across different requests, even though their computation excludes other candidates. This is different from both independent bi-encoding and Jeva’s immutable option memory. The reported residual permutation flips also distinguish a structural design objective from exact numerical behavior. Its frozen contrastive baseline uses a different training setup, so that comparison does not isolate attention structure alone.

Prism-1 uses the same separation of a shared causal prefix and isolated candidate blocks, but scores each candidate with the native language-model head’s yes/no log odds at its final token (Teng et al., 2026). A softmax across these scores produces the choice distribution; LoRA and candidate cross-entropy adapt the model without a separate learned scalar head. Every candidate starts at the same position offset. For a fixed prefix and deterministic computation, isolation and position reuse make scores independent of candidate serialization order and preserve pairwise odds when unrelated candidates are added. The latter is a restriction as well as an invariance: a task requiring an existing option’s score to change with its rivals needs a different dependency structure.

C.3 Supervision and the Target Distribution

Takeaway 3. The supervision source determines what a fitted decision distribution represents.

Labels describe outcomes in the training population, contrastive pairs distinguish matched inputs from chosen negatives, and teacher probabilities reflect the teacher’s information and computation. Similar cross-entropy expressions can therefore fit different quantities.

Observed and mixed-label supervision.

Jeff adds a residual decision head to the original letter readout and trains that head with backbone LoRA using cross-entropy (Geuter et al., 2026). The supervision mixes ordinary dataset labels, human uncertainty and ordinal annotations, and teacher-provided soft distributions. It is neither a pure hard-label recipe nor an RL method. Per-type temperature fitting follows training. The calibrated frozen model already provides a strong reference on the authors’ decision benchmark, while their knowledge-oriented comparisons still favor Jev. These results motivate a strong baseline; they do not establish equivalence across workloads.

The adapted LLM-as-Jev variant instead preserves the architecture and candidate suffix representation (Li and Wagle, 2026). Its training loss uses a locally normalized candidate-prefix tree plus KL anchors that preserve the frozen model’s behavior on legal/illegal token mass and outside decision positions. That locally normalized training distribution should not be confused with the globally normalized suffix likelihood in Equation (8). The recipe uses public human-annotated training data rather than teacher-synthesized labels and studies both full adaptation and LoRA.

Kev illustrates supervised adaptation with a different readout. Its pointer head projects the decision position and each option boundary into a shared space and normalizes scaled dot products over options. The released recipe uses cross-entropy; smaller models use LoRA, while the documented 27B model uses full-parameter adaptation.88 8 Official implementation and recipe: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev. Optional permutation and ordinal losses exist in the code but are not part of the documented released-model recipe.

Intern-Decision instead retains the native vocabulary head and fits hard-label, full-vocabulary cross-entropy only at shifted decision positions (Zhu et al., 2026b). Its input contains the complete ordered schema and an assistant JSON skeleton with <decision> placeholders. The logits immediately before each placeholder predict that field; earlier placeholders remain visible without feeding back gold or predicted answers. Inference restricts these logits to legal options and applies temperature scaling. The language parameters are adapted while the vision encoder and projector remain frozen. Training over the full vocabulary and restricting the inference readout are distinct operations, and the shared causal pass does not imply independence or order invariance across fields.

Modality-specific readouts.

MJev-Spatial reuses pretrained query/key projections from the final full-attention layer to match a decision state to option-end states, rather than adding a prediction head (Qin et al., 2026). Mean scaled inner products across query heads become logits for one candidate softmax. The retained language parameters are trained with cross-entropy while the vision encoder and merger are frozen. Because option states come from a causal sequence, later options can see earlier ones; shuffling options during training does not establish structural permutation equivariance.

Qwen-Audio-Jev uses a different design: a shared audio–language prefix state feeds three affine heads for 64 Choice indices, one binary Noul logit, and ten ordinal Score indices (Fang et al., 2026). Candidate meanings are specified in the input, and each categorical head is normalized over the valid indices. Supervised training updates the audio encoder, adaptor, backbone, and heads using the observed primitive’s loss: Choice cross-entropy, binary cross-entropy, or ordinal cross-entropy with cumulative-distribution and expected-index penalties.

Contrastive state–action alignment.

Contrastive Language Models (CLM) use a frozen Qwen3-8B encoder with learned state and action projection heads.99 9 Original technical blog: https://contrastive-lm.notion.site; official implementation and reference-model recipe: https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM. Matched state–action pairs supervise bidirectional InfoNCE: the state retrieves its matched action and the action retrieves its matched state among batch alternatives. At inference, state plus instructions and each candidate are encoded independently, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives the candidate distribution. Independent candidate representations can be cached, although different question instructions change the state encoding. This is learned contrastive alignment rather than teacher-probability distillation.

Reasoning-endpoint distributions.

SII-Decision trains a direct readout against a same-size backbone’s reasoning-conditioned predictions (Duan et al., 2026). For each question, two reasoning chains yield two candidate distributions; their mean becomes the cached student target.1010 10 JEVal Section 6.2 specifies a nonthinking-readout fallback for invalid chains, while Appendix F.4 describes excluding truncated, invalid, or top-option-disagreeing chains from added-source training data. Cross-entropy to this target is combined with a KL constraint to the original nonthinking prediction, and ordinal tasks also use an expected-level penalty. The student updates language layers while retaining the original label head, and inference uses a single prefill with no generated rationale. This is offline reasoning-to-readout self-distillation, not student on-policy rollout distillation.

Where SII retains reasoning-endpoint probabilities, LDM constructs soft targets from sampled answers (Chen et al., 2026b). In the primary experiments, its SPRD variant draws four reasoning answers from a frozen Qwen3.8-27B teacher for all student sizes and forms a vote histogram normalized by the number of parseable answers. SPRD already requires the top vote share over all four samples to reach 0.750.75; SPRD-C additionally requires the majority to agree with the label intended during data construction. This checks consistency, not independent correctness. The LDM objective uses supervised NLL on one record type and weighted teacher-to-student KL on another, rather than applying both losses to every example.

Endpoint averaging and answer counting differ as estimators, but need not estimate different quantities. If both use the same rationale distribution ρ⁡(r∣x)\rho(r\mid x) and answers are sampled categorically from the same endpoint distribution q(⋅∣x,r)q(\cdot\mid x,r), then

𝔼r∼ρ[q(y∣x,r)]=𝔼r∼ρ,a∼q(⋅∣x,r)[𝟏{a=y}].\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\rho}[q(y\mid x,r)]=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\rho,\,a\sim q(\cdot\mid x,r)}[\mathbf{1}\{a=y\}]. (9)

Averaging conditional probabilities removes the final-answer sampling noise under these assumptions. Different teachers, prompts, decoding rules, or sample filters can change the target marginal; Equation (9) does not establish equivalence between the actual SII and LDM datasets.

Full-depth predictions as a teacher.

Teacher computation can also differ in depth rather than in the use of reasoning traces. FunDM freezes the backbone and trains a decision head on an intermediate hidden layer to match the full-depth model’s distribution using KL(pteacher∥pstudent)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{teacher}}\|p_{\mathrm{student}}) (Panchal, 2026). Inference can stop before the remaining layers, although the new head still requires training.

Black-box imitation of the deployed service.

AutoTrust-JEV-27B uses output distributions obtained from TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as its main supervision stream.1111 11 Author model card and recipe: https://huggingface.co/autotrust/JEV-27B. Its training corpus also contains programmatic labels and downweighted uniform-placeholder targets. The documented recipe fits LoRA adapters and a decision head using target-to-student KL, with an ordinal ranked probability score (RPS) term. The service-target component is behavioral imitation of a black-box model. Agreement with that teacher is a different outcome from correctness against independent labels, and it does not identify the teacher’s internal training algorithm. External-teacher models such as Eikos and Torchcast provide further distribution-fitting variants, catalogued in Appendix I.

These teacher targets differ in the information and computation they retain (Figure 33).

Workflow-specific supervision.

Some models are trained to support a particular workflow. LAVOIR adds slot representations and a value-of-information head to Laya, trained with decision cross-entropy and value regression (Yilmaz et al., 2026). The final recipe sets the inherited RL weight to zero. The model learns both a decision distribution and estimates used by the ask/decide/handoff policy in Appendix E.2.1.

AgentDecision-4B, introduced in JevAgentHarness, trains the decision component on agent states (Zhu et al., 2026a). Its Qwen3-4B LoRA recipe includes post-error states from mistake replay. When Jev’s top option matches the gold label, the supervised target mixes 0.30.3 gold one-hot mass with 0.70.7 teacher probabilities; otherwise it uses the gold label alone. Cross-entropy plus a Brier term precedes closed-loop GRPO with a fixed LLM, task-success and cost/error rewards, and a KL anchor to the supervised model. Here environment feedback updates the decision model itself. Appendix E.3 examines the different role of a fixed Jev service guiding another learner.

C.4 Statistical Objectives and Gradient Credit

Takeaway 4. The probability objective and the random variable receiving credit are separate choices.

A proper probability score defines an objective for truthful reporting; a gradient estimator determines how its training signal reaches the parameters. For a distribution pp and outcome yy, log score log⁡py\log p_{y} and negative Brier score −∑k(pk−𝟏[k=y])2-\sum_{k}(p_{k}-\mathbf{1}[k=y])^{2} reward truthful probability reports in expectation. A differentiable readout can optimize either score directly. By contrast, rewarding only a sampled answer’s correctness maximizes ∑kpk​qk\sum_{k}p_{k}q_{k} under outcome distribution qq, generally favoring a mode of qq rather than reporting qq. Thus the word “RL” identifies neither the statistical property being optimized nor an advantage over direct proper-score fitting.

Figure 34 contrasts direct differentiation, output-space perturbations, and rationale-policy credit. OpenJev-RLCD, the rationale-policy method depicted here, retains generated reasoning at inference; this is a property of that method rather than a requirement of every rationale-based training procedure.

Output-space policies.

Laya and Chinese-Jev perturb output logits and apply policy-gradient updates in that space; Chinese-Jev combines soft cross-entropy with Gaussian perturbations around detached logits and a group-baseline estimator (Wang et al., 2026c). This does not require a generated chain of thought. The decider-derived this-that-model combines CE and Brier terms with a sampled-outcome Brier reward and a control-variate estimator (Cheng et al., 2026b). Another output-policy variant, decider-2B v10, uses PPO over environment actions with terminal returns and an auxiliary proper-log-score belief objective; the documented 4B and 35B releases do not use that RL stage.1212 12 Version-specific recipe: https://github.com/Mapika/decider/blob/main/docs/RL.md. These methods apply stochastic policy updates in output space rather than over generated reasoning. Their estimators, stop-gradient choices, and rewards determine what those updates contribute beyond direct fitting.

Qwen-Audio-Jev makes this distinction explicit with an importance-weighted, pairwise sampled-action estimator for negative Brier score and ordinal RPS (Fang et al., 2026). Its exploration mixture, leave-one-out baseline, and detached weights yield the direct proper-score gradient in expectation under the stated construction. Thus the estimator need not define a different probability target from direct fitting. This equivalence does not establish an empirical advantage in variance, efficiency, or calibration.

Reasoning-token policies.

OpenJev-RLCD first calibrates an answer distribution conditioned on sampled rationales, then adds REINFORCE credit to the rationale policy using the same proper score (Gao and Wang, 2026). If

J(θ)=𝔼r∼πθ(⋅∣x)[S(pθ(⋅∣x,r),y)],J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}[S(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,r),y)], (10)

then its two relevant gradient paths are the differentiable readout term and the score-function term through πθ​(r∣x)\pi_{\theta}(r\mid x). Stage one uses the former; stage two adds the latter, with a baseline and KL regularization. Its main experiments score each rationale’s distribution separately and retain explicit rationales at inference. It is an independent RLCD interpretation, not a disclosed implementation of proprietary Jev.

StartLux combines instant decision learning with an AutoThink variant that allocates reasoning conditionally (Zhuang et al., 2026). Its instant model makes full-attention layers bidirectional while retaining causal linear-attention layers. RLCD2 uses a frozen reference model’s before/after probability signal to train a reasoning-token policy. Within groups containing only nonempty traces, the initial-score term cancels under reward centering; empty traces receive zero reward, so this cancellation does not extend to arbitrary mixed groups. PostHog’s Jeeves is another reasoning-policy implementation: its repository combines supervised learning, CISPO-style updates, a pointer head, and a diffusion drafter. Its documented reward uses correct-answer probability with a length penalty, which should not automatically be called a proper scoring rule.

Appendix D Executing Decision Models

The readouts and learning recipes above leave several execution choices open. A direct choice can follow different computational paths and undergo serving transformations. Figure 35 contrasts computation shared across questions (a–b) with computation adapted within a decision (c–d). Both affect cost, while routing and output transformations can also change the returned prediction.

D.1 Direct Outputs and Adaptive Computation

Takeaway 5. The absence of a returned rationale does not imply a fixed computation budget.

A direct student may omit its teacher’s reasoning, an intermediate head may omit later layers, and a recurrent model may perform additional hidden steps without generating text. Conditional reasoning introduces another possibility, mixing direct and deliberative requests behind one interface. These choices change different resources, so generated-token count alone cannot compare their computational demands.

Conditional reasoning changes both the path and the prediction.

LDM routes low-margin items to the student’s untuned base for one reasoning rollout and adopts its answer; the direct branch keeps the readout’s answer (Figure 35c; Chen et al., 2026b). Its threshold is the validation margins’ 30th percentile, which does not fix the routed fraction on unseen data. StartLux AutoThink instead uses the same model weights for the initial causal readout, reasoning, and endpoint readout (Figure 35d; Zhuang et al., 2026). With a maximum initial probability below 0.90.9, it generates up to 4,096 reasoning tokens and returns 0.25​p0+0.75​p10.25p_{0}+0.75p_{1}; otherwise it returns p0p_{0}. These routes differ in the model called, the trigger, and the returned prediction.

Hidden computation and selective reasoning.

Latent loops allocate extra computation without generating a textual rationale. SanSi repeatedly applies a recurrent backbone and reads a decision distribution after each loop (Gan et al., 2026). The base weights are frozen, while shared LoRA adapters and loop-specific readout corrections are learned. Cross-entropy and Brier losses supervise the loop outputs, with gradients passing through preceding loops. The paper trains with eight loops and evaluates different loop counts. Latent computation thus varies separately from parameter count and generated-token count, and additional loops need not improve every task.

Selective Reasoning instead exposes three control decisions: when to start generation, when to read a partial rationale, and when to accept the current answer (Zheng and Chen, 2026). A reader is trained on empty and partial reasoning prefixes using a frozen backbone. The start gate estimates correction benefit relative to regression risk, the read scheduler limits costly reader calls, and the accept rule uses the reader’s distribution. An accepted prefix answer cancels generation only if generation is still active. If no prefix answer is accepted, a terminal read returns an answer without a certainty requirement. Thus the entropy threshold governs early acceptance rather than guaranteeing the confidence of every returned answer. The threshold itself measures distribution concentration, not an independently measured probability of correctness.

FastJEV changes the execution of an existing decision model without weight training (Ma et al., 2026a). It reuses shared context and recurrent states, forks candidate-prefix caches, and selects a candidate-path layer-skipping mask using relative-score perturbations on unlabeled calibration inputs. These mechanisms preserve the context and candidate inventory while changing the work performed on candidate paths. Prefix reuse can reduce computation yet increase latency through execution overhead. Its results therefore support a serving analysis under specified workloads, rather than a universal latency improvement. The OmniJev model evaluated in that paper should not be conflated with the separately named OneJev repository.

Comparing these paths requires accounting for backbone depth, reader calls, generation, caching, and scheduling. Returned-answer length alone does not measure their cost.

A single-pass primitive can form a sequential predictor.

MJev-Spatial illustrates a further distinction between the primitive and the completed prediction (Qin et al., 2026). A categorical answer uses one decision, while spatial point prediction uses three successive nine-way cell choices. The first two choices determine new crops from the original image, which are re-encoded for the next stage. Training packs teacher-forced stages into one backbone pass, but inference must follow the predicted crops sequentially. The spatial quantization bound assumes the correct cell choices; it is not a bound on model prediction error. Single-pass training, single-pass primitive scoring, and single-pass task inference are therefore separate claims.

D.2 Serving and the Returned Prediction

Takeaway 6. Serving choices can change prediction semantics as well as execution cost.

The model head is only one stage of a deployed prediction. Postprocessing can move its probability mass, scalar reduction can retain different information, and question batching can change how computation is shared. Behavior observed through a service can therefore reflect transformations applied after training as well as the learned distribution.

Sharing computation across questions.

The same typed interface can expose different question-processing graphs. Kev’s documented hybrid-backbone implementation processes separate causal question rows and can reuse a state cache in serving (Figure 35a). Cloudflare Clef instead uses a joint schema head and describes one forward pass for all questions (Figure 35b). Jeff’s released server evaluates questions serially, while official Jev describes shared-state parallel question processing. These differences determine how computation is shared even when each question returns the same output type.

Documented readouts do not always identify a training recipe. Perplexity’s decider v1.1 describes a separate 255-row readout and saved temperature calibration, but the public model cards for decider and Clef do not specify their training objectives (Appendix I). JevK5 further describes a one-pass readout only up to its candidate limit and a multi-pass tournament beyond it. Candidate limits and question organization are therefore necessary conditions for interpreting an execution claim.

Transforming the returned prediction.

Jeff illustrates how postprocessing can change the apparent decisiveness of a model. Its default binary “commitment” transformation moves intermediate probabilities beyond the benchmark’s abstention interval. The returned distribution therefore differs from the temperature-calibrated distribution before this transformation, and an evaluation of calibration must specify which one it measures. Reduced abstention under this rule cannot be attributed to the cross-entropy training objective alone.

SII returns the expected ordinal level, whereas Jeff’s released scalar field returns an argmax level. Identical categorical distributions can therefore yield different scalar answers.

Table 2 relates learning recipes to their readouts and public artifacts.

Appendix E Decision Models in Downstream Workflows

Execution determines the cost and form of a returned decision; its consequence depends on where it intervenes in a task. We distinguish control of an ongoing trajectory, selection among completed outcomes, acquisition of evidence, and assistance to another learner. These roles carry different error and recovery costs, even when they use the same decision model.

E.1 Controlling a Trajectory or Selecting Its Outcome

Takeaway 7. Action control and completed-run selection affect different parts of a trajectory.

Online selection changes which state the agent reaches next. Completed-run selection instead chooses among trajectories whose generation cost has already been incurred. Both can use a fast scorer, but only the former changes the actions within an individual run. This distinction determines which generator, candidate budget, and executor must remain fixed to attribute a downstream gain to the decision component.

Online action selection.

Jev Ultrafast constructs a dynamic action space from the observed browser state.1313 13 Primary implementation: https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast, especially “The action space” and “Evidence and limits.” Each observation supplies an indexed table of elements. A single Jev request asks for both an operation and speculative targets for the supported operation types. The executor uses only the target corresponding to the selected operation (Figure 36a). A small LLM supplies text when the operation requires typing. Ordinary code checks target compatibility and page freshness, executes the action, and obtains the next observation.

The division of labor depends on enumerating actionable choices from the environment. The decision model selects within that interface, while generation remains available for open-ended content. Selection of a DONE action still needs an independent outcome check. The repository reports a small set of demonstrations and repeated runs on one browser task; these establish an implemented loop, not general reliability or an isolated effect of the decision model.

JevCoder exposes a related boundary in code repair (Zhang et al., 2026). Its components recommend code snippets, guide action types, and judge whether to submit or continue. When Jev selects an action type, an LLM still generates the specific command. A judge that blocks a command does not thereby supply a better one, and some blocking interventions hurt performance. The full-workflow experiments are separate from component studies on selected success/failure panels; they should not be pooled as a single task-success estimate. Each full-workflow task receives one run per condition, which limits what can be inferred about repeated-run variability.

Decision gates within a larger controller.

A decision gate can replace a local choice, advise a generator, reject an action, trigger extra work, or escalate uncertain cases. JevAgentHarness implements these roles at tool selection, bounded arguments, memory operations, reflection, stopping, and model routing (Zhu et al., 2026a). Its deployment cascade compares the maximum option probability with thresholds fitted for each decision point using held-out shadow trajectories and intervention costs. Free-form arguments still require an LLM. The gate’s confidence and the harness’s policy jointly determine behavior; a threshold alone does not establish safe execution. The same work also trains a decision model and evaluates controllers, which are distinct contributions (Appendices C.3 and F).

Jev-LiteMAS specializes this division of labor to a predefined pool of generative experts (Wang et al., 2026a). Jev selects the next expert or, when eligible, STOP, and screens artifacts for acceptance or escalation. On escalation, an LLM reviewer supplies a verdict and textual feedback; an expert revises the artifact, which is then screened again. The decision model does not generate repair instructions, and local artifact acceptance is distinct from stopping the entire workflow. Savings therefore depend on the escalation frequency and on whether the resulting artifacts still satisfy the task.

Jarvis applies typed control to an asynchronous task ledger (Wang et al., 2026b). Runtime code constructs eligible operations tied to task identifiers and versions; the decision model selects among them from the transcript, history, and ledger. Low-confidence cases delegate to a worker without speculative ledger mutation. Code enforces one live version, rejects stale results, revalidates plans, and requires a playback receipt before marking speech as delivered. These invariants belong to the executor, not to the model’s probability estimates. The paper also trains a separate audio LISTEN/DIRECT/DELEGATE gate; that learned gate and the downstream ledger policy should not be treated as one training mechanism.

A penetration-testing harness study illustrates how several decision roles can coexist in one domain (Barbosa, 2026). Typed decisions support finding adjudication, severity assessment, agent pruning, and bounded confirmation, while the harness retains evidence gates and execution. Its exploratory comparison uses one run per condition on one target, and subsequent retests change the harness. The study demonstrates this division of labor, but the separate effects of the decision model and harness remain unresolved. Establishing a benefit would require comparing the same task decomposition and execution policy with alternative decision components.

Selecting completed runs.

CLM and FunDM move the intervention from actions within a run to selection among completed coding-agent runs. If the generator produces trajectories τ1,…,τN\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{N}, a scorer chooses

ı^=arg⁡maxi∈{1,…,N}​vϕ​(τi).\hat{\imath}=\arg\max_{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}}v_{\phi}(\tau_{i}). (11)

The generation cost of all NN candidates remains part of the workflow. A cheap verifier may reduce selection overhead, but this alone does not make the total procedure cheaper than generating one run.

CLM’s released coding verifier averages state--action cosine scores over the last twelve trajectory steps by default.1414 14 Official selector implementation: https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM/blob/main/evaluation/bon_eval.py. The coding evaluation uses domain adaptation; it is distinct from the general typed-question interface. This aggregation is a use of the contrastive scorer, not the softmax over a caller’s candidate menu described in Appendix C.3. FunDM uses a separately trained coding-agent head to judge a whole run (Panchal, 2026). Its MCQ head and coding head are distinct, and the repository distinguishes the whole-run judge from an action-trained FunDM-CE variant.1515 15 FunDM implementation and reproduction notes: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM. Figure 36b therefore shows a shared selection operation with different scoring mechanisms. It does not imply shared heads, training data, or directly comparable reported performance.

E.2 Changing the Evidence Available to a Decision

Takeaway 8. Clarification and memory control alter the information available to subsequent decisions.

The preceding workflows use the available evidence to choose behavior or an outcome. Clarification obtains an external answer, while memory control changes how past evidence is organized and retrieved. These operations can improve a later decision without changing the decision model’s parameters. Their benefits and costs therefore depend on the information acquired, as well as the quality of the local probability report.

E.2.1 Acquiring Missing Information

LAVOIR predicts the value of acquiring missing information. It extends the open Laya model so that a forward pass returns both a temperature-scaled decision distribution pp and values v^k\hat{v}_{k} for unasked information slots (Yilmaz et al., 2026). For a gold decision y∗y^{*}, the target and bounded prediction are

tk=p^k​(y∗)−p^0​(y∗),v^k=stopgrad⁡(1−∑ypy2)​σ​(hk),t_{k}=\hat{p}_{k}(y^{*})-\hat{p}_{0}(y^{*}),\qquad\hat{v}_{k}=\operatorname{stopgrad}\!\left(1-\sum_{y}p_{y}^{2}\right)\sigma(h_{k}), (12)

where p^0\hat{p}_{0} and p^k\hat{p}_{k} come from the same frozen, temperature-scaled snapshot before and after a sampled answer to slot kk. The value head produces hkh_{k}, and σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. The detached Gini factor bounds predicted values when the current decision distribution is concentrated. Training regresses v^k\hat{v}_{k} toward tkt_{k}, with both normalized by the target standard deviation, alongside decision cross-entropy. The final recipe sets the inherited policy-gradient weight to zero. Multiple complete profiles for a partial message make the regression estimate an expected gain under the sampled answers. Thus the learned value is a proxy whose validity depends on the frozen predictor and answer distribution. This construction is a model contribution, while the use of its outputs defines the interaction.

At runtime, the policy asks about k∗=arg⁡maxk⁡v^kk^{*}=\arg\max_{k}\hat{v}_{k} when v^k∗>c\hat{v}_{k^{*}}>c and the question budget remains. The question comes from a slot template. Its answer is appended to the state, which is then re-encoded; an already asked slot is not repeated. If no question is taken, the policy hands off when 1−maxy⁡py>ch1-\max_{y}p_{y}>c_{h} and otherwise returns the most probable decision (Figure 36c). Here cc and chc_{h} are the asking and handoff thresholds. Single-pass prediction within a turn does not make the entire interaction a single-pass procedure.

Clarification changes the source of information available to the model. LDM and StartLux conditional thinking process the existing input through an internal rationale, whereas LAVOIR obtains an external answer. It also goes beyond deferring low-confidence cases by ranking particular missing fields by predicted benefit. The evidence is strongest for synthetic multi-turn dialogues, with limited real single-exchange tests and one training seed. Comparisons against slower value-of-information computation and an LLM agent remain incomplete, leaving open whether the learned acquisition policy offers a better quality–cost trade-off across interaction settings.

E.2.2 Controlling Memory Construction and Retrieval

Jev-Mem places a decision controller between stored observations and an LLM answerer (Jiang et al., 2026). Its contribution is the organization of memory operations around fast typed decisions, rather than a new recipe for training the controller. Shared canonical memory nodes participate in semantic, temporal, causal, and entity relation views. Figure 37 separates writing this memory from retrieving evidence, because the decision objects and feedback loops differ.

Writing preserves observations and judges relations.

Incoming observations retain their original text and provenance. The controller annotates overlapping memory characteristics, while deterministic vector, lexical, entity, and time search produces a bounded set of candidate neighbors. The controller then judges inferred relations; thresholds determine which edges are added. Reliable timestamp ordering and exact identifiers can be handled directly by code. Thus the normal write path does not ask the model to irreversibly discard observations before their future relevance is known. Maintenance may mark redundancy, contradiction, or obsolescence while retaining original evidence, and textual abstraction can be escalated to an LLM.

Retrieval adapts both where to search and when to stop.

Given a query, the controller predicts relevant relation views, multi-hop needs, and recency, which guide budget allocation. Hybrid vector and lexical retrieval supplies anchors. During retrieval, the controller assesses whether accumulated evidence is sufficient and whether further expansion is likely to help. If needed and within budget, bounded graph expansion proposes candidates, which are scored and added to the evidence set. The loop stops on sufficient evidence, low expected additional benefit, or a resource limit. Selected memories then go to the LLM for answer synthesis. The controller affects evidence acquisition; it does not replace the final generative answerer.

The reported evaluation uses LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini as the answer model and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring. These results concern Jev-based control on LoCoMo and do not evaluate the Laya controller or LongMemEval configuration provided by the implementation.1616 16 Jev-Mem implementation: https://github.com/libingzheren/Jev-Mem. Separating write and read control is particularly useful for attribution: changing stored relations can affect later answers even if the query-time controller is held fixed.

Evidence expansion without a preconstructed graph.

SAG2 instead starts from a local SQLite FTS5/BM25 index, without corpus-time embeddings or a neighbor graph (Wu, 2026). Jev makes a binary Noul judgment about each passage’s necessary contribution to a supported answer chain, conditioned on the retrieved evidence. This is not a single global Choice over passages. Ordinary code extracts lexical expansion terms from scored seed passages; retrieval and evidence-conditioned rescoring can repeat within a bounded budget. Local diversification then produces the final evidence set. The experiments evaluate retrieval rather than generated answers, and development includes MuSiQue and a synthetic enterprise corpus. The local index does not make the complete system local, because the evidence scorer uses the hosted Jev service. Relative to Jev-Mem, the intervention moves from constructing and traversing stored relations to building query-time evidence chains through lexical expansion.

E.3 Decision Models in Agent Learning

Takeaway 9. A decision model can guide another learner without itself being trained.

A fixed decision service can also change an agent’s exploration, rewards, or updates during learning. Any resulting benefit may persist in the trained agent after the service is removed. This differs from fitting a replacement decision model to service outputs, as in Appendix C.3, where training changes the model that will answer future decision requests. The relevant distinction is which model learns from the service and what it learns to do.

Ma et al. (2026b) use Jev as an action-policy reference, an exploration source, an auxiliary reward assessor, and a replay-priority signal. These interventions change an agent’s data or updates, so their success is measured in the learned agent. AutoTrust instead fits a replacement decision model to Jev’s probability outputs, making reproduction of the teacher’s predictions a training target.

The interventions have different semantics. Policy assistance supplies actions that can be imitated or compared with the learner’s actions by a critic. Exploration assistance replaces some random actions with Jev suggestions. Reward assistance maps rubric judgments to bonuses or gates. Replay assistance reweights stored experience using Jev judgments. The reported replay variant omits importance correction and therefore intentionally changes the effective training weighting. None of these roles makes an ordinal judgment a validated cardinal Q-value merely by converting its label to a number.

Information access also matters: Jev can receive structured descriptions beyond the learner’s own observation, and the trained learner can later be deployed without Jev or its auxiliary rewards. The paper’s MiniGrid and Atari experiments provide evidence for particular learning interventions, with three seeds; replay assistance does not uniformly help. The resulting gains or losses concern how the service changes learning. They cannot be attributed to the quality of its decision probabilities without separating added information, changed exploration, and changed objectives.

Joint learning changes the decision model as well as the agent.

Dyad spans both levels in a different way (Zhan et al., 2026). Its language model retains token generation and switches to a typed action distribution at designated interaction positions. The model aligns state and action representations through projector training, then applies environment-reward policy optimization over token and action decisions. Its action encoder may be updated alone or jointly with the state encoder. Action features are reusable only while their environment context and descriptions remain unchanged. Thus the learned architecture belongs to model construction, while the interleaving of language and environment actions defines the downstream workflow; it is not simply a frozen service plugged into another learner.

Appendix F From Local Probabilities to Workflow Reliability

These workflow roles call for separate tests of candidate probabilities, selected actions, and complete task outcomes. Accurate probabilities can yield a poor action under an unsuitable decision rule; a correct local action can still fail to secure task success. Our experiment measures selections, leaving calibration and downstream utility unresolved. The studies below identify the evidence needed to connect these levels.

F.1 Local Probability Quality and Decision Utility

Takeaway 10. Calibration, distribution fidelity, and decision utility are distinct.

Ordinary calibration compares reported probabilities with outcome frequencies among cases receiving the same predicted probabilities. Subgroup calibration additionally requires this agreement within specified groups. Distribution fidelity instead asks whether the complete prediction matches the conditional target for each input. Neither calibration nor fidelity alone specifies the action taken or the cost of an error. A decision rule converts probabilities into behavior, so a utility improvement can arise from a better distribution, a better rule, or both. Comparisons must separate these changes before attributing a gain to learning.

Known distributions separate probability estimation from sampled correctness.

ProbabilityBench supplies simulated problems with a known conditional distribution p∗p^{*} given the visible input (Dai et al., 2026). This permits direct comparison with p∗p^{*}, rather than treating one sampled answer as the complete probability target. Accuracy evaluated in expectation under these conditional targets is bounded by the Bayes accuracy for the same visible information. Accuracy against sampled test labels can exceed that reference through label-sampling noise. For a predicted distribution qq, the input-averaged KL(p∗∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p^{*}\|q) equals excess expected log loss relative to p∗p^{*}. A constant class prior satisfies ordinary calibration while ignoring input-specific information, and need not be calibrated within subgroups. Finite-bin estimates can also hide canceling errors or reflect sampling noise. Exact uncertainty in a synthetic generator is therefore valuable evidence about probability estimation, but does not establish access to the true uncertainty of an arbitrary real task.

Additional computation can sharpen probabilities without improving calibration.

SanSi provides a concrete example of why compute allocation and probability quality must be evaluated together (Gan et al., 2026). Its later loops continue to increase confidence even after most answers have stabilized. On the 9,645 answerable test items, the 1.4B model’s expected calibration error rises from 0.082±0.0100.082\pm 0.010 at loop three to 0.093±0.0120.093\pm 0.012 at loop eight. These are means and standard deviations over three training seeds, using ten equal-width confidence bins. The comparison concerns different readout depths within each trained model. It shows that additional latent computation can worsen calibration even within the trained loop range, so a stopping rule needs evidence for the probability or decision objective it serves.

Utility also depends on the decision rule.

TypedBench complements this view with policy-generated cases, controlled framing changes, and cost-sensitive evaluation (Sharma et al., 2026). Its calibration and stress-test protocols distinguish benign framing sensitivity from adversarial perturbation. A change from argmax to the Bayes action under a cost matrix changes the decision rule; the resulting utility improvement cannot all be credited to better calibration. Synthetic labels make some controls possible while limiting direct conclusions about unconstrained natural tasks.

Benchmark scores depend on their evaluation protocol.

Published scores differ in both what they measure and how evaluation informs model development. JEVal supplies a benchmark as well as the SII model discussed in Appendix C.3, but the SII release’s separate evaluation suite does not reproduce that benchmark protocol (Duan et al., 2026). Inner Jev’s Capability metric differs from ordinary accuracy, and its OpenDecisions results inform recipe selection (Geuter et al., 2026). LLM-as-Jev likewise uses public JevBench errors to guide data-mixture development (Li and Wagle, 2026). Metric definitions and evaluation feedback must therefore be accounted for before these scores can support a common ranking.

Data overlap and execution conditions further limit comparisons. FunDM’s reproduction notes disclose overlap between a CLM post-training collection and its test collection. Local-model and hosted-API latency also reflect different hardware and network conditions. Generalization and efficiency claims therefore require controls beyond matching the reported metric.

F.2 Composition and Input Sensitivity

Takeaway 11. Reliable isolated decisions need not remain reliable under composition.

An isolated prediction tests one input and output interface. Composing predictions introduces dependencies; changing a request can alter evidence, eligible actions, or numerical computation. Interpreting sensitivity first requires specifying what should remain invariant. Our permutations preserve question content and candidate identities, whereas adding a candidate or revealing evidence can change the decision problem.

Coherence studies test probability relationships across related questions (Joy, 2026), while option-set studies test how predictions respond to changed alternatives (Rajput et al., 2026). Neither relationship follows from calibration on isolated questions.

Request context, candidate eligibility, and numerical precision.

Chen (2026) distinguishes changes to the questions bundled into a request, the evidence provided, and the eligible candidates. A model whose question compiler produces exactly the same input can be invariant for that reason, whereas a full-schema prompt exposes other questions to the decision computation. The Nimble intervention removes other questions from the prompt and eliminates the observed flips, but is not length-matched. Small Laya shifts largely disappear at higher precision or after rounding. The observed sensitivity can therefore reflect prompt construction or numerical precision as well as architectural dependencies. Conditional odds between retained alternatives separate genuine relative-score movement from the inevitable change in a softmax denominator. When a readout restricts the vocabulary, its allowed-label mass provides additional information lost by normalization.

From correct choices to correct sequences.

Choice2Seq compares native candidate choice with independent-position and serial-prefix output interfaces on paired problems (Lai et al., 2026). Its serial correctness retention is P⁡(serial correct∣native correct)P(\text{serial correct}\mid\text{native correct}), not agreement with the native answer or fidelity to a plan. Cases improved by the serial interface and the marginal accuracies are needed alongside this conditional statistic. Gold-copy and self-plan controls address different fidelity questions. Candidate restrictions can also change the available search space and number of calls, so a composition claim requires the relevant interface and information controls.

Robustness and program consequences.

Robustness studies connect input sensitivity to the consequences of a valid but incorrect choice. DecisionRobust tests label-preserving perturbations and targeted prompt injection on initially correct decisions across text and vision (Lan et al., 2026). The distinction between observation text and task instructions matters because changing task facts would change the decision problem itself. JevProbe traces the structured response through application logic and tests whether reachable lower-trust context can redirect a program decision while leaving task facts and code fixed (Luo et al., 2026). Together, these studies show why schema validity is insufficient for reliable execution. They identify failures of input handling and decision use, with modeled program consequences rather than measured real-world losses.

The released response can reveal more than the intended decision.

TUPLE-Bench studies whether a response about an authorized coarse category reveals a protected finer mechanism in the model’s private evidence (Yang et al., 2026). Choice-only, confidence, full-probability, and native-response releases are derived from the same saved response, separating release policy from model reruns. Its informed decoder receives the gold coarse category and two known fine-grained hypotheses; this is a passive closed-set audit, not an estimate of unrestricted real-world leakage. A separate legitimate consumer sees neither private evidence nor those hidden labels. The proposed workflow-conditioned probability quantization selects codewords that preserve a frozen consumer’s actions, including clarification, with a native-response fallback when no match exists. It can preserve wrong actions as well as correct ones, so action preservation establishes neither improved task quality nor a confidentiality guarantee. The contribution concerns evaluation and release postprocessing, not a new decision-model training objective.

F.3 Complete-Workflow Outcomes

Takeaway 12. Task-level gains depend on the surrounding policy and its total resource use.

Ling et al. (2026b) separate changes to the action interface from changes to the decision model in ALFWorld. They compare the original baseline, an LLM using a Choice interface, and Jev using that interface. The first contrast examines the candidate-selection interface; the second compares decision components within it. Their AndroidWorld experiments compare baseline and Jev integrations without this three-way control. Across these workflows, local decision savings do not uniformly translate into better task outcomes. Action granularity also differs in one integration: FastAgent-J takes one tool action per step while its baseline can take multiple actions. The study thus provides evidence about particular integrations while illustrating the controls needed to interpret them.

JevAgentHarness distinguishes isolated multiple-choice accuracy, decisions on recorded agent states without execution, and actual closed-loop intervention (Zhu et al., 2026a). Its closed-loop tool-selection comparison lets the LLM supply tool arguments and uses unthresholded replacement. That protocol differs from the confidence cascade proposed for deployment, so its outcomes cannot be attributed directly to that cascade. Scripted acceptable actions in DecisionGym and disjoint rollout seeds also do not, by themselves, establish generalization to unseen task distributions.

System1-Arena broadens the comparison across static decisions and closed-loop environments under task-specific shared harnesses (Chen et al., 2026a). Candidate construction converts otherwise open-ended search, patches, or arguments into finite alternatives; the reported results are conditional on this interface. The static comparison uses 85,305 questions across 94 tasks, a subset of the released collection, and excludes its game and embodied questions. Reported static scores weight tasks equally, with source averaging within a task. Closed-loop scores weight environments equally. For real-time simulations, the environment advances using each model’s measured median latency while retaining the prior action, rather than measuring each call’s realized delay inside the simulation. Probability extraction also differs across native decision models, verbalized-probability APIs, and local label-logit models. These protocol choices enable useful controlled comparisons while limiting a universal ranking across interfaces, hardware, and workloads.

Adoption is a separate object of measurement.

Ecosystem studies explain where decision models are used, but do not replace these capability and workflow evaluations. Ling et al. (2026a) analyze public Jev repositories by application domain and decision purpose. Purposes can overlap within a project, and repository counts or stars measure ecosystem activity rather than model quality or methodological novelty. Tang and Zheng (2026) audit early typed-decision-model evidence and connect it to label-probability readouts, reranking, calibration, and model cascades.

Appendix G Open Questions

The unresolved question is which design changes preserve correct choices across equivalent presentations. The comparisons below separate representation, learning, computation, and workflow effects so that any improvement can be attributed to a specified intervention.

Which improvements survive equivalent presentations and related decisions?

Takeaways F.1 and F.2 distinguish local probability quality from consistency across requests. The main study finds substantially more Jev variation under reordering than under fixed-order repetition, without identifying the mechanism behind this difference. Independent studies examine disagreement between direct and hierarchical predictions (Joy, 2026), option-set dependence (Rajput et al., 2026), serial correctness retention (Lai et al., 2026), and the limited transfer of local savings to successful agent outcomes (Ling et al., 2026b). Together, they motivate testing whether a local probability improvement persists under transformations that preserve the intended decision problem and predicts utility in a fixed workflow. The intended invariance must be specified first. Independence of irrelevant alternatives is not universally appropriate, since an added option may provide meaningful context or change the task. Prompt serialization and precision require controls (Chen, 2026), while cacheability must be separated from set-dependent refinement (Li and Wang, 2026).

When does the gradient estimator matter beyond the target and objective?

Takeaway C.4 separates statistical supervision from the variable receiving gradient credit. Replacing observed labels with teacher distributions changes the target; adding output noise can replace an unperturbed score with its expectation under perturbation. An estimator comparison therefore requires a fixed objective and perturbation distribution, with pathwise differentiation and score-function credit compared where both apply. Matching the backbone, prompt, candidates, examples, adaptation budget, and validation split would isolate this question, with frozen and temperature-calibrated readouts as starting controls. Whether a gain survives common calibration and probability postprocessing would help establish its source. A negative result would delimit the value of a specified stochastic update without resolving how proprietary Jev is trained.

Which aspects of reasoning transfer into a direct readout?

Takeaways C.3 and D.1 distinguish the information supplied during learning from the computation available at inference. JEVal reports that reasoning-to-readout transfer differs between evidence-weighing and computation-heavy tasks (Duan et al., 2026); earlier System 2 distillation also documents task-dependent transfer (Yu et al., 2024). Conversely, theoretical work shows that some computations can be internalized under particular architectures and curricula (Huang et al., 2026). The unresolved empirical question concerns the interaction of training support, novel rule composition, and dependency depth. Correct-label supervision, additional data, intermediate-state hints, and explicit-reasoning controls would help distinguish imperfect targets and learning limitations from residual computational demands. Failure on a task family alone does not prove an impossibility of single-pass reasoning.

When does a better decision model improve the complete workflow?

Takeaways E.1–E.3 identify where a model intervenes; Takeaway F.3 shows why that intervention matters for evaluation. A comparison within a fixed workflow can replace only the decision component while holding candidate construction, retrieval, budgets, fallback rules, and answer generation constant. A complementary comparison retains the same model while changing its role or control policy. Jev-Mem motivates separating write control from read control; run selection requires matching candidate-run generation; LAVOIR requires accounting for newly acquired information and the cost of questions. Crossing model and workflow choices can reveal whether local probability improvements transfer to task outcomes and how that transfer depends on the surrounding policy. Existing evidence does not establish that either model quality or workflow design universally dominates.

These factors can interact. Establishing a structural advantage requires identifying both the intervention and the conditions under which its benefit survives.

Appendix H Survey Synthesis

A candidate-distribution interface accommodates different representations, objectives, gradient estimators, inference procedures, and downstream roles. The main study shows that this shared interface does not ensure preservation of correct choices under reordering. Explaining the observed differences requires controlled comparisons under common information and resource budgets, followed by tests of whether local improvements benefit the workflow the model controls.

Appendix I Extended Public Implementation Inventory

Table 3 summarizes additional implementations and the mechanisms documented in their primary sources as of October 19, 2026. Public artifacts do not by themselves establish independent reproduction.

Documented readout, undisclosed training objective.

Cloudflare Clef attaches a small transformer joint schema head to Qwen3.8-27B. Its card describes all-question probabilities from one forward pass, an expected-value scalar score, and backbone, head and inference artifacts, but not the exact post-training objective. pplx-decider-v1.1-27b uses a separate 255×5120255\times 5120 readout, noncausal full-attention layers with unchanged linear-attention behavior, and saved temperature calibration. Its training loss and update method remain unspecified. These interfaces alone establish neither RL nor supervised training.

Additional documented implementations.

imajev documents language LoRA with frozen vision and weight-space averaging of a hard-question adapter with its soft-target continuation. jqv offers frozen-logit backends and trainable slot or pointer heads with LoRA and CE plus Brier loss. openJev-verdict describes a marker-pointer distribution head, an out-of-fold confidence head, and symmetric KL between option-shuffled training pairs.

Other designs vary the candidate representation. jevlike learns option-conditioned context scoring with either a learned byte encoder or a frozen pretrained encoder. agent-jev combines independent candidate paths with a permutation-equivariant scoring head and documents soft CE plus Brier training for AgentJev-0.6B. GLiNER2.5-Decide publishes supervised fine-tuning formats and procedures, but the objective used for its released weights remains unspecified. jev-local offers an optional frozen-model log-probability scorer and a deterministic default stub; head training is explicitly deferred.
